title: Palm fibres, coiled form: reading Moroccan basketry closely
deck: A close look at how palm fibres become structured vessels, and at what museum objects and living-heritage documentation can responsibly tell us about Moroccan basketry.

hero_media.creator: RoubinakiM
hero_media.title: Traditional colourful Moroccan baskets
hero_media.alt_text: Colourful handmade palm-fibre baskets displayed in a market in Marrakesh, Morocco

sources.title: Al Saafiyat and plant fibres: craft and social traditions — 2026 nomination material
Māktaf: coiled palm-leaf basket from Morocco — collection record

sections.heading: A vessel begins as a plant
sections.text: Palm-leaf basketry turns flexible plant material into a load-bearing form through repeated coiling, wrapping and joining. The finished basket is useful, but it is also a record of material selection, hand pressure and accumulated skill.

sections.heading: The living material
sections.text: The documented objects use palm fibres rather than a generic idea of natural fibre. Leaves are gathered, dried and divided into workable elements; wool or other fibres may wrap the structural core in coloured market baskets.

sections.heading: How structure is built
sections.text: Coiled basketry grows in a spiral. A bundle forms the core while a wrapping element binds each new pass to the previous row. Small changes in tension, spacing and the angle of the coil determine the wall and rim.

sections.heading: Documented context, not a single origin story
sections.text: UNESCO’s current multinational nomination documentation includes Moroccan practitioners and objects within a wider set of plant-fibre traditions. That supports a living practice, but not a claim that every Moroccan basket shares one technique or history.

sections.heading: What museum records can show
sections.text: A museum collection record can preserve dimensions, materials and acquisition context for an individual basket. It cannot, by itself, describe the full working knowledge of a maker or prove that a historic object represents current practice.

sections.heading: What the evidence does not establish
sections.text: These sources do not justify claims that all palm-fibre work is environmentally benign, unchanged through time or made by one culturally uniform group. Responsible interpretation stays close to the named object, place and documentation.
